editorNote: A weekly record of computers, games and digital culture.
morningLine: Elite looks toward new machines as Britain’s cartridge business contracts.

lead.headline: British Telecom’s Firebird wins the rights to take Elite to Z80 computers
lead.dek: Spectrum version promised; Amstrad conversion probable as Elite heads for Firebird’s premium line.
body: British Telecom’s Firebird has obtained the rights to convert Acornsoft’s Elite for Z80 computers. Popular Computing Weekly reports the agreement in its November 29 issue, following an auction the previous week. The price is described as a substantial sum but is not disclosed.

The option covers the Spectrum, Amstrad CPC 464, MSX and the awaited Enterprise. That breadth is not a production schedule: Jacqui Lyons of Marjacq Scripts, representing authors Ian Bell and David Braben, confirms a Spectrum version and says a CPC 464 edition is probable. No firm MSX conversion plans are reported.

Elite is destined for Firebird’s gold premium range rather than its silver budget range. The report anticipates a Spectrum edition around April or May 1985 at about £15. Those figures remain expectations; there is no Spectrum release to buy this week.

For players watching the BBC and Electron space-trading hit from other keyboards, the agreement promises a wider flight deck. The immediate news is a licence and a confirmed conversion commitment, not a finished fleet of ports.

stories.headline: Coleco and Parker Brothers retreat from the British games market
body: Coleco and Parker Brothers are retreating from the British games business, according to this week’s Popular Computing Weekly. Coleco’s Philip Gibbs says involvement with ColecoVision will not continue; an agency is to handle software support for existing owners.

Console stock remains in shops through Hyde Park Clothing Company. A reported inventory figure is disputed by its manager, so no firm total can be given. Ideal Toys says it intends to put less emphasis on electronics and more on Cabbage Patch Dolls and educational toys.

Parker has withdrawn its 1984–85 British product programme, though its spokesman does not necessarily regard the retreat as permanent. The period report points to falling Atari VCS prices, premium cartridge prices and Britain’s small Commodore disk market. These are UK withdrawals, not announcements that either company has closed worldwide.

stories.headline: LaserJet wins a 119-printer showdown as laser output reaches the PC desk
body: PC Magazine’s November 27 special issue tests 119 printers, and Alfred Poor places Hewlett-Packard’s LaserJet at the front of the field. This is a comparative review of an existing product, not a launch announcement.

The $3,495 serial-interface printer uses a Canon copier-derived laser engine, produces 300-dot-per-inch output and carries an eight-page-per-minute rating. Poor measures an 18-second wait for the first page, followed by about 7.5 seconds per page: short letters and sustained printing are different speed tests.

A replacement cartridge costs $99 and is said to last about 3,000 pages. Optional ROM cartridges add fonts. Setup earns praise, font-selection controls less so; supplied graphics screen-dump support is for the HP-150, not the IBM PC. The reviewer observes discounts below $3,000 without identifying a dealer.

stories.headline: Home bulletin boards become a social network—and an arcade
body: Home bulletin boards are becoming meeting places and game rooms. Kathy Yakal’s November COMPUTE! report visits Chicago-area Atari users and reports at least 20 Atari boards in the metropolitan area. John Semenek began his board for a user group.

Stan and Susie Subeck’s Valley Girl BBS supplies adventures and trivia along with Valspeak menus. On this board, delete becomes bag and exit becomes de-val. The play described is hosted board entertainment, not evidence of simultaneous multiplayer.

Running a board costs money and time. Ric Manning’s survey reports average startup spending above $3,000, around $50 in monthly expenses and maintenance that can reach 50 hours a month. Most home boards take one caller at a time; passwords, membership fees and rules against copyrighted-software uploads are increasingly part of the sysop’s job.

stories.headline: Borland sells a pop-up desk—and charges extra for an unprotected disk
body: Borland’s Sidekick advertisement offers IBM PC-family users a small desk that pops up while another program runs. Its tools include a notepad, calculator, calendar, phone directory, auto-dialer and ASCII table.

The November 27 advertisement demonstrates a notepad over Lotus and describes capturing screen information into notes and transferring calculation results into underlying software. Auto-dialing requires a Hayes Smartmodem or compatible.

The standard advertised edition is $49.95. A non-copy-protected version costs $79.95, with $5 shipping and handling: a $30 premium for an unprotected disk. These are advertising claims and quoted prices, not independent performance-test results.

computerItems.title: Sinclair Spectrum portable project
computerItems.summary: November 29 PCW pp.1,5 reports confirmation of a battery-powered Spectrum-compatible portable with flat display, single microdrive, CMOS RAM and proposed £300 price. Display development means launch not expected before mid-1985; this is a proposal, not released hardware or a retrospective identification as the Z88.

briefs.headline: One caller at a time
briefs.summary: November COMPUTE! contrasts single-user home BBSs with large multi-user commercial services such as CompuServe. Busy signals and long-distance charges shape home telecomputing.

briefs.headline: COMDEX’s sober mood puts pressure on the PC business
briefs.summary: November 20 COMDEX report gives earlier-month context: record 1,400 exhibits but a restrained mood; the show is not redated into the target week.

briefs.headline: Doomdark’s Revenge
briefs.summary: November 29 PCW p.1 says the Lords of Midnight sequel is now in shops, available so far only for Spectrum at £9.95. Morkin has been kidnapped by Shareth, Doomdark’s daughter; Luxor, Rorthron and Tarithel must rescue him. This is a dated availability report, not an exact launch-day claim.

briefs.headline: Elite conversion agreement
briefs.summary: Firebird obtains Z80 conversion rights; Spectrum edition planned for April–May 1985 around £15. No released Spectrum port this week.

briefs.headline: Reflection
briefs.summary: Sean Puckett’s November COMPUTE! p. 58 type-in reversi game supports one player against the computer or two players. Versions: Atari 24K, Commodore 64, unexpanded VIC-20, TI-99/4A 16K with regular BASIC, Apple, IBM PC with 64K/BASICA/CGA, PCjr with Cartridge BASIC, and Color Computer with Extended Color BASIC. Joystick required for Atari, C64, VIC and Color Computer.

market.headline: Britain’s cartridge trade retrenches
market.summary: Coleco and Parker withdraw British programmes while Firebird invests in home-computer conversions. Parker’s spokesman leaves open the possibility of a return.

worldAnchor.headline: Britain and Spain agree on Gibraltar movement and talks
worldAnchor.summary: Britain and Spain agreed in Brussels on November 27 to reciprocal rights, free movement and talks including Gibraltar sovereignty. The agreement was not an announcement that the frontier reopened that day.

bbsNote.headline: 300 or 1200 bps? Home callers weigh cost against speed
bbsNote.summary: November COMPUTE! supplies both a modem buyer’s guide and named BBS reporting. All entries below are editorial paraphrases of published reporting, not recovered BBS messages.

posts.text: Sharon Darling describes common 300- and 1200-bps modems; faster transfers reduce hourly service and long-distance costs, while Jerry Hussong argues local casual BBS use can still justify 300 bps.
Kathy Yakal reports adventures and trivia hosted by Stan and Susie Subeck, alongside Valspeak menus.
Ric Manning’s survey puts average initial BBS spending above $3,000 and ongoing costs around $50 monthly, with as much as 50 hours of monthly maintenance.
Kent Fillmore proposes an area-code franchise network with space for local user groups; only his home pilot is documented as operating.

posts.topic: Proposed QL network and modular modem
posts.text: PCW November 29 reports very early negotiations for a QL-only network, developed by Prism, and a QL-dedicated modem due at January’s Which Computer Show. Richard Hease stresses planning, not a live service; modular prices are £79.95, £79.95 and £39.95.

curiosity.headline: A Valley Girl board lets you bag a message and de-val
curiosity.summary: A genuine November 1984 Atari BBS gives online computing a Valley Girl accent.
curiosity.detail: Stan and Susie Subeck took inspiration from their 13-year-old daughter’s Valspeak. Their Chicago-area Valley Girl BBS substitutes bag for delete and de-val for exit, includes a slang glossary, and offers adventure games and trivia. Kathy Yakal reports it in COMPUTE! issue 54, p. 46.

items: Magazine publication dates establish reporting dates, not necessarily transaction or launch dates. Firebird auction occurred the previous week; Spectrum Elite, Sinclair portable and QL network/modem remain forecasts or plans.
December CGW remains adjacent-period context, not evidence of availability in this week. No independently established non-computer gadget breaking news or era-defining milestone: both omitted.
Byte, InfoWorld and Softalk not exhaustively inspected; expanded original Popular Computing Weekly coverage resolves the earlier exact-week gaming gap.
Existing primary-source research, Billboard transcription and film/world-news findings retained; no invented scene names or recovered BBS messages.
